overview: **Simulated, balanced profiles:** these 243 miner interviews are model-generated cases, not survey evidence or population estimates.
**AI Plateau** leaves most shifts in place, while existing pay, mine and household risks still worry some.
Shorter AGI timelines spur **training and job moves**; more warning gives time to save, though hands-on roles remain exposed.

S0.headline: Most miners keep working under AI Plateau, while old worries about bills, mine closures and equipment trials remain.

whatTheyDo.text: Keep operating trucks, loaders and drills on the current roster, as Iris Fischer would at Red Hollow.
Put money aside for rent or a lost shift, as Pedro Lopez plans at fifty a week.
Use small tools for drill patterns or work notes, as Diego Walsh plans during breaks.
Bring pay and contract demands to union meetings, as Iris Fischer plans for the March agreement.
Watch a tool for several complete shifts before using it more widely, as some operators propose.

whatTheySay: **Mine work** still needs a person in the cab or at the face, even if routine forms get quicker.
**Pay, prices and closures** matter more to many miners than a small AI change.
whatTheyThink: **Relief** about AI coexists with rent, mortgage or shift worries already present.
Some expect **driverless trials or mine closures** to continue even if thinking AI stalls.
Others see **steady pay and saved time**, though a few wanted a faster route into new work.
howTheyFeel: **Calm** is common among miners with steady shifts and a financial buffer.
**Unease or anxiety** persists where thin savings, contracts or household income are already exposed.

differences.text: Mean mood (1 calm, 5 panicked) is 2.73 for 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.06 for 81 strong-cushion profiles.
Learning AI appears in 45 of 81 adaptive profiles’ plans, versus 1 of 81 resistant profiles’ plans.
The 81 mid-career profiles average 1.99 on the five-point worry scale, versus 1.62 for 81 early-career profiles.

quotes.name: Iris Fischer
quotes.text: Nothing changes for the drivers, and nothing changes in my bank account either. Two weeks of rent saved is still two weeks of rent saved.

quotes.name: Rosa Olsen
quotes.text: I already ask an AI to explain every alarm code on my dozer, and it's still me pushing the dirt.

quotes.name: David Nakamura
quotes.text: A delayed tyre order worries me more than a clever office tool.

thoughts.text: My mine work looks steady in this picture.
My thin savings or tight bills make even a small setback hard.
I still watch mine prices, closures, cuts, or existing automation.
My savings give me room and choices.
My junior standing or unfinished learning still matters.

least.name: Buffered operators
least.story: The calmest profiles usually describe steady hands-on shifts and money saved for ordinary interruptions.

most.name: Thin-buffer households
most.story: The most worried face tight bills, uncertain shifts or scarce local jobs even with only small AI changes.

S1.headline: Steady Disruption sends miners toward new tools and training as office automation makes slower robot adoption feel closer.

whatTheyDo.text: Learn mine software or AI study tools, as Yara Rossi does for remote operations.
Keep paid shifts while building another skill, as Nikhil Kowalski does alongside a drone course.
Press for retraining and job-transfer clauses, as Iris Fischer plans through her union.
Apply for a control-room or electrical course, as Pedro Lopez and Diego Walsh plan.
Skip purchases and cut bills, as Iris Fischer plans by selling the old car.

whatTheySay: **Office planning** changes first, while trucks, drills and dozers still need operators for now.
Miners ask for **paid training and fair access** to remote or technical roles before crews shrink.
whatTheyThink: Many see **robotics** reaching their own seat after software reshapes dispatch and planning.
Some see a **route into remote work**, while others fear the control room will hold fewer people.
A tighter **household budget** makes even a slower transition urgent for some.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** is the most common mood as miners picture fewer operators or hours.
A small **calm group** sees a chance to use technical skills or expand work.

differences.text: Learning AI appears in 78 of 81 adaptive profiles’ plans, versus 8 of 81 resistant profiles’ plans.
Average worry is 2.91 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.20 among 81 strong-cushion profiles.
Early-career profiles average 2.28 in worry, versus 2.75 for mid-career and 2.64 for late-career profiles; each has 81 cases.

quotes.name: Iris Fischer
quotes.text: The office goes first and the trucks come after. I'm the newest driver with a dented record, so I know whose name sits at the top of the list.

quotes.name: Esther Abbott
quotes.text: I'm a bad dozer driver but a good student, so a mine full of software might actually suit me better.

quotes.name: Iris Novak
quotes.text: A few minutes of waiting is cheaper than a collision.

thoughts.text: My paid shifts or wage could shrink as software spreads.
Robots could take my hands-on job later.
AI could change planning and other screen-based jobs.
I could move into remote operations or learn the new systems.
I expect software plans and targets to change my work or safety.
My hands-on mine work looks safe for now.

least.name: Technical openings
least.story: The calmest profiles name a technical role, remote work or business opening they could use as tools change.

most.name: Fragile paid shifts
most.story: The most worried see mine hours or roles shrinking while household bills still depend on that pay.

S2.headline: AGI by 2028 threatens office and control-room plans before capable robots reach hands-on work around 2031.

whatTheyDo.text: Train for maintenance, care or another trade, as Diego Walsh plans with an electrical apprenticeship.
Seek work outside the mine, as Grace Evans plans by exploring hospital or care roles.
Cut household bills, as Iris Fischer plans by reviewing every expense with her partner Tom.
Keep taking paid shifts while looking ahead, as some operators plan until robot equipment arrives.
Push for redundancy pay and retraining support, as Pedro Lopez plans through his union.

whatTheySay: Miners distinguish **2028 planning changes** from capable hands-on robots around 2031.
Miners want **income and training support** while they still have paid shifts.
whatTheyThink: The **control room** may disappear before operators can use it as an escape from the cab.
By around **2031**, robots could take the driving, drilling and loading work that still pays them.
Three years may be too short to **build savings or qualify** for different work.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety and alarm** dominate; three profiles report panic in this snapshot.
Even miners with savings fear **two wages or a whole town** could be hit together.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.83 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 3.15 among 81 strong-cushion profiles.
The 81 resistant profiles average 3.70 in worry, versus 3.27 among 81 adaptive profiles.
The 81 high-standing profiles average 3.31 in worry, versus 3.59 among low-standing and 3.56 among mid-standing profiles.

quotes.name: Iris Fischer
quotes.text: Two years of warning is no warning for someone like me. I'd be 32, with a truck licence for a truck that drives itself.

quotes.name: Rosa Olsen
quotes.text: My plan was to be the person who watches the robots, and in two years the AI watches the robots.

quotes.name: Liam Reyes
quotes.text: I have a list of cuts, but it does not replace a wage for three years.

thoughts.text: My hands-on mine job or paid shifts could disappear.
Thinking AI could threaten my planning or screen-work options.
My savings, debt, or household bills leave little room for lost wages.
My final earnings or pension could change my retirement plans.
I have some time or options to prepare for a different skill.

least.name: Workers with a route
least.story: The least worried still expect disruption but can name savings, another job or training to use while paid work continues.

most.name: Little room to move
most.story: The three panicked and 112 alarmed profiles fear lost mine pay, short savings or scarce alternatives before they can change course.

S3.headline: AGI by 2031 gives miners more time to train and save, though the later robot date still threatens their paid work.

whatTheyDo.text: Train for electrical, repair or other work, as Nikhil Kowalski plans with an instrumentation certificate.
Keep earning mine pay while preparing, as Grace Evans plans while finishing her dozer ticket.
Move toward council, repair or technical work, as Carla Chen plans with a roads-crew enquiry.
Build a cash buffer, as Tara Petrov plans by saving truck pay toward a year of costs.
Watch the self-driving drill trial before choosing another trade, as Femi Yilmaz plans.

whatTheySay: **Five years’ notice** gives workers a chance to learn and save while the mine still pays them.
A **course needs a real job** at the end, not just a certificate.
whatTheyThink: A longer runway makes **trade training** more practical, especially while wages still arrive.
Some fear **screen jobs disappear in 2031** and physical jobs follow around 2034.
Others doubt they can **afford a course** without paid time or a job offer.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety** remains the most common mood despite the extra time.
Some feel **uneasy or calm** with time to act; 15 profiles remain alarmed.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.09 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.44 among 81 strong-cushion profiles.
The 81 resistant profiles average 2.95 in worry, versus 2.59 among 81 adaptive profiles.
Retraining appears in 71 of 81 early-career profiles’ plans, versus 49 of 81 late-career profiles’ plans.

quotes.name: Iris Fischer
quotes.text: Eight years sounds like plenty, but I know myself. I'd spend the first four telling everyone the driverless trucks will never work in our dust.

quotes.name: Rosa Olsen
quotes.text: Five years is enough to get one step ahead of the machines, if I start the day I hear about it.

quotes.name: Iris Novak
quotes.text: I will not resign until I have the pension figure in writing.

thoughts.text: I can use the warning to prepare another work path.
I still need wages and time to ease household costs.
I am thinking about when automation changes mining work.
I expect desk or screen tasks to change early.
I need evidence that replacement jobs will exist and last.
I need to check retirement money before I stop working.

least.name: Workers with options
least.story: The three calm and 65 uneasy profiles often cite savings, paid training, another role or a possible retirement route.

most.name: Short of options
most.story: The most worried see time passing while savings, training funds or local vacancies remain uncertain.

S4.headline: A decade before AGI lets more miners keep earning and build a route out, but current money pressures persist.

whatTheyDo.text: Keep working on current equipment while it pays, as Femi Yilmaz plans with his drill.
Save from mine wages, as Iris Fischer plans through payroll each fortnight.
Complete a trade or technical course over several years, as Pedro Lopez plans in diesel fitting.
Move into repair, care or technical work, as Elena Diaz plans with a dealership role.
Wait for evidence from nearby robot trials before changing work, as Felix Garcia proposes.

whatTheySay: **Ten years** offers room to learn a trade, build savings or approach retirement.
Miners still want **paid paths into work**, since a long warning does not guarantee a new job.
whatTheyThink: Many can **earn and save** while hands-on roles continue toward the later robot date.
Some see **time to retrain**, while others worry a course may lead to a job AI also takes.
Thin savings or current bills do not disappear just because the **deadline is distant**.
howTheyFeel: **Unease** is most common as miners plan around a distant but real end point.
Some feel **calm** with savings or retirement in sight; others remain anxious about present income.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.78 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.46 among 81 strong-cushion profiles.
Retraining appears in 54 of 81 early-career profiles’ plans, versus 2 of 81 late-career profiles’ plans.
The 81 resistant profiles average 2.25 in worry, versus 1.91 among 81 adaptive profiles.

quotes.name: Iris Fischer
quotes.text: Ten years is enough time to fight properly. I'd want the union to win a written promise that drivers get trained into the new jobs first.

quotes.name: Rosa Olsen
quotes.text: Ten years of warning is a gift, and I'd hate to be the one who wasted it sitting in a dozer.

quotes.name: Liam Reyes
quotes.text: I would want pension and housing costs on paper before moving to a cheaper home.

thoughts.text: I can use the longer runway to prepare another path.
I can use more years of current work to support my plans.
I see risks to my work or preparation during the long wait.
I need proof that new work will remain available.
I need to check household money before deciding when to retire.
I may still need paid work despite the longer wait.

least.name: Long-range planners
least.story: The calmest profiles describe savings, steady work, a funded change or retirement they may reach before robots spread.

most.name: Bills before robots
most.story: The most worried still face thin savings, uneven pay or uncertain retirement income long before capable robots arrive.
